rv.q: Cera is a different kind of Warren — gawkier, more vulnerable and perhaps with his devastating timing, even funnier — in a tale that exposes the bad ideas hatched by kids with more energy than they know what to do with.
The acrobatics being performed in Anna D. Shapiro’s sensational, kinetically charged revival of Kenneth Lonergan’s “This Is Our Youth” aren’t anything like those you’d find at the Cirque du Soleil.
Spending two hours watching these wealthy, unmoored slackers is a treat, even without the contact high.
That we end up caring so much for her — and Warren, and Dennis — is why this show works so well.
And yet Lonergan has created three surprising character studies -- complete with individual peculiarities and universal problems -- that find genuine life onstage again.
This Is Our Youth is rich and sad and wry in its cruel-to-be-kind portrayal of disillusioned adolescents struggling to take up the business and onus of grown-up life.
A starry cast blazes in this dark, wistful winner.
For a static period piece that’s all talk and no action, Lonergan’s plotless play is a charmer.
It’s enough to see those ideas enacted, as we do, for instance, when Dennis excuses his constant bullying by telling Warren: “We all talk that way, it doesn’t mean anything.”
Gevinson will not take Broadway by storm with this performance — which is probably the best thing for this huge young talent in the long run.

Unfortunately, much like the characters, the intimate play seems somewhat adrift in this much larger venue featuring an elaborate, overblown apartment building setting that seems to dwarf the action below.
This might have to do with fine performances that nonetheless fail to connect.
There’s little that’s wasted in this Youth.
He's at the top of his game in his 1996 play "This Is Our Youth," now running at the Cort Theatre in a terrific revival.
Culkin is sensational as Dennis, a talkative schemer whose occasional stumbles in no way impede his innate sense of self-confidence.
Hysterically funny and heartbreakingly sad, this is anything but a wasted Youth.
The interplay of narcissism and insecurity in Dennis’ monologues shows Lonergan at his best, and Culkin does the playwright full justice.
The incontrovertible fact is, he has written the play, and it's a worthy one.
Even so, it suits his character and he brings plenty of laughs.
Sadly, Gevinson, who plays Jessica, is the production's weak link.
Later, his personality undergoes an abrupt shift, which is one of several unpersuasive aspects of the production.
In spite of it all, I walked out of the two-acter curiously unfulfilled.

cn.t: Lonergan's 1996 slacker drama gets a kinetically charged Broadway revival with strong performances from Cera, Culkin, and Gevinson, though some find the period piece's portrait of privileged aimlessness more dated than resonant.

sg.ra: JEJ is one of Broadway's smallest houses (1,063-1,092 seats across sources) and seats 101-112 in Center Orch rows AA-A put you almost nose-to-stage; SeatPlan and Headout both name seats 105-109 in AA-A as the single best spots. Mezz overhang doesn't bite until Row J, so Center Orch stays clean of ceiling cutoff all the way back to Row I.

SeatPlan explicitly calls out 'Rows E to J in the Center Orchestra are cheaper than premium with a good view,' and because JEJ's auditorium is unusually compact even Row J sits closer to the stage than mid-orch in bigger Shubert houses. This is the sweet spot before the Mezz overhang obscures the top of the stage (SeatPlan: cuts in after Row O; TickPick: overhang begins Row J but worsens deeper).

sg.vl: Overview pick with an elevated head-on
sg.ra: JEJ Mezz is one of Broadway's smallest (264-275 seats) and sits directly above the stage per SeatPlan: 'every row facing directly above the stage.' SeatPlan notes the Balcony overhang at Mezz Row B 'doesn't affect views' and the railing height doesn't obstruct (TickPick). Good rake means heads-in-front is a non-issue. AVFMS April 2024: 'View was fantastic, person in front didn't obstruct my view.'

sg.vl: Underrated value if you skew center
sg.ra: Unusual for Broadway, TickPick explicitly states JEJ 'does not have obstructed view seats on the sides of the orchestra and mezzanine' thanks to the small footprint and no pillars. But SeatPlan warns double-digit seats at the far side and Boxes above 16 are angled with stage right partially obstructed, so you want the low-numbered seats closer to center aisle.
sg.rr: L Mezz A-G odd 1-25; R Mezz A-G even 2-26; plus 24 box seats

sg.vl: Cheapest tier, steepest price in comfort
sg.ra: SeatPlan: Balcony is 'very steep and cramped compared to the lower two seating areas,' ~2 steps down per row with three flights of stairs (Shubert: 55 steps total or elevator post-renovation). SeatPlan flags Row H as 'isn't as well-raked as the rest of the section,' so the back row both loses rake AND inherits the steep climb. JEJ balcony is unusually high — Shubert's own description puts it behind Row F entrance.
sg.rr: A-G (L/R) / A-H (Center); 283 seats plus 12 box seats
